lessons.title: Subject and Object Markers — 이/가, 을/를
lessons.explanation: Korean uses particles (조사) attached to nouns to show their role. Subject markers: 이 (after consonant) / 가 (after vowel). Object markers: 을 (after consonant) / 를 (after vowel). The verb always goes at the END.
examples: 고양이가 물고기를 먹어요. (The cat eats fish.)
학생이 책을 읽어요. (The student reads a book.)
저가 한국어를 배워요. (I learn Korean.)
친구가 음악을 들어요. (My friend listens to music.)
lessons.tip: Choose 이/을 after a consonant, 가/를 after a vowel. Practice with common nouns until it's automatic.

lessons.title: Topic Marker — 은/는
lessons.explanation: 은/는 marks the topic of the sentence (what you're talking about). Use 은 after a consonant, 는 after a vowel. It often contrasts or emphasizes: 'As for X…' Korean is an SOV (Subject-Object-Verb) language.
examples: 저는 학생이에요. (As for me, I am a student.)
한국어는 어려워요. (As for Korean, it is difficult.)
커피는 좋아요. (As for coffee, I like it.)
오늘은 날씨가 좋아요. (As for today, the weather is good.)
lessons.tip: 은/는 often implies contrast: 나는 먹었어 (I ate) implies 'but someone else may not have'.

quiz.question: Which form of the topic marker comes after a consonant?

lessons.title: Polite Speech Level — -요 Ending
lessons.explanation: Korean has multiple speech levels. The most useful for beginners is the polite informal level, marked by -요 at the end of verbs and adjectives. It is appropriate for most daily conversations with adults who are not close friends.
examples: 먹어요 (I/you/he/she eats) — eats (polite)
공부해요 (I/you study) — studies (polite)
예뻐요 (It is pretty) — pretty (polite)
학교에 가요. (I go to school.) — polite
lessons.tip: The -요 ending is used for all persons and tenses in context — you can say 먹어요 and the context tells you who is eating.

quiz.question: What ending marks polite informal speech in Korean?

lessons.title: 이다 — To Be (Copula)
lessons.explanation: 이다 (to be) connects a subject to a noun predicate. Polite form: 이에요 (after consonant) / 예요 (after vowel). Formal: 입니다. Negative: 이/가 아니에요 (is not).
examples: 저는 학생이에요. (I am a student.)
이것은 책이에요. (This is a book.)
그것은 사과예요. (That is an apple.)
저는 선생님이 아니에요. (I am not a teacher.)
lessons.tip: 이다 is not a verb but a copula (connector). It attaches directly to the noun without a space.

quiz.question: How do you say 'This is a book' formally in Korean?

lessons.title: Location Particles — 에 and 에서
lessons.explanation: 에 marks static location (where something is/exists) or destination (where you're going). 에서 marks the location where an action takes place.
examples: 학교에 가요. (I go to school.) — destination
집에 있어요. (I am at home.) — static location
도서관에서 공부해요. (I study at the library.) — action location
학교에서 친구를 만났어요. (I met a friend at school.) — action location
lessons.tip: Key test: If the verb is 있다/없다 (exist) or a movement verb, use 에. If it's an action verb, use 에서.

quiz.question: Which particle marks where an action takes place?

lessons.title: Connective Endings — -고, -(아/어)서, -(으)면
lessons.explanation: Korean connective endings join clauses. -고: 'and' (sequential or simultaneous). -(아/어)서: 'so' / 'because' / 'and then' (causal). -(으)면: 'if' / 'when' (conditional).
examples: 밥을 먹고 잠을 잤어요. (I ate and then slept.) — -고
비가 와서 집에 있었어요. (It rained so I stayed home.) — -(아/어)서
시간이 있으면 전화해요. (If you have time, call me.) — -(으)면
공부하고 놀아요. (I study and play.) — -고
lessons.tip: -(아/어)서 cannot be used with past tense before it — the tense marker goes on the final verb only.

lessons.title: Honorific Infixes and Speech Levels
lessons.explanation: Korean has elaborate honorific system. The infix -(으)시- is added to verbs to show respect for the SUBJECT. Vocabulary also changes: eat → 드시다 (honorific) vs. 먹다 (plain). Speech levels: formal polite (-습니다/-ㅂ니다), informal polite (-아/어요), plain (-아/어), informal (-아/어).
examples: 선생님이 가르치세요. (The teacher teaches.) — -(으)시-
할아버지가 드세요. (Grandfather is eating.) — honorific verb
어디 가세요? (Where are you going?) — polite + -(으)시-
사장님, 말씀해 주세요. (Please speak, director.)
lessons.tip: Use -(으)시- whenever you respect the subject — with teachers, elders, customers, and bosses.

quiz.question: What infix shows respect for the subject in Korean?
